one_liner: LZ77 codec for small cache/record values whose hand-written per-CPU decoders read 14-83% faster than liblz4.
what_it_does: Packs and unpacks individual values (aimed at 512 B to 64 KiB records in caches and key-value stores) in its own self-describing stream format: the stream carries its uncompressed length but no frame, magic, checksum or dictionary. It also decodes raw LZ4 blocks, since its even token split is LZ4's layout. The C API is four calls over caller-owned buffers (lzvolt_compress, lzvolt_declared_size, lzvolt_decompress, lzvolt_decompress_lz4); compress returns 0 to mean 'not worth packing, store the bytes as they are'. It is not a drop-in for the LZ4 API, and its own streams are not LZ4 blocks.
how_it_is_fast: Byte-oriented LZ77 (64 KiB window, minimum match 4) with two token bit splits; a value may switch from one split to the other once, which the author measured at about 19% on shapes whose match lengths overflow the narrow field. Decoding uses separate hand-written GAS assembly bodies per CPU part line (Xeon, EPYC, SSSE3-only x86, generic AArch64, Neoverse V2), chosen once per process from CPUID or MIDR, with unchecked wide copies behind an up-front validation pass. The measurement log credits the big wins to removing work: memcpy for long literal runs (+34% on noise_64k), one wide token load replacing three dependent loads (+37%), and an output slack margin (lzvolt_decompress_bound) that lets the last copy run full width.
when_to_use: Read-heavy caches or record stores that compress each value separately, roughly 512 B to 64 KiB, where decode latency per value matters more than ratio.
JSON-like records with repeated keys: the measured shapes are synthetic JSON records, decoded at 7-13 GiB/s of output on Xeon 8481C, EPYC 9B14 and Neoverse V2.
Stores that already hold raw LZ4 blocks and want a faster reader without rewriting data (ahead of liblz4 on 20 of 27 measured cells).
Linux or macOS on x86-64 or aarch64, where the assembly decoders are used.
Rust services (crate lzvolt 1.0.0) or C/C++ code willing to link a Rust staticlib/cdylib through include/lzvolt.h.
when_not_to_use: You need interoperability: the native format is readable only by lzvolt (a conforming LZ4 decoder rejects some streams), and there is no frame, checksum or streaming mode.
Large files, archives or values over 2^29-1 bytes (536,870,911): the format caps value size and was tuned only on 512 B to 64 KiB values.
Windows or other architectures: they get the portable Rust decoder, which is slower and was not benchmarked against liblz4.
Incompressible small blocks in LZ4 format: noise_512 in LZ4 blocks loses 15% (Xeon) and 12% (EPYC) to liblz4, and the kernel is sensitive to buffer placement there.
You need ratio comparisons against zstd, LZAV or other fast codecs on standard corpora: only liblz4 and lz4_flex were compared, on generated data.

integration.form: crate (also staticlib and cdylib with a hand-written C header; prebuilt glibc, musl and macOS libraries with lzvolt.pc and a CMake package config on the v1.0.0 release)
integration.dependencies: none at run time; building needs a Rust toolchain and a C compiler/assembler (cc crate in build.rs); system liblz4 only for the comparison benchmarks and interop tests (feature liblz4)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 (rust-version and rust-toolchain.toml); C callers need C99 stdint.h
integration.platforms: x86-64 and aarch64 on Linux and macOS with assembly decoders; Windows and every other target build the portable Rust decoder
integration.thread_safety: Header states every function is thread-safe with no shared state; the compressor uses a per-thread scratch buffer.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — lzvolt_decompress_lz4 reads raw LZ4 blocks (like LZ4_decompress_safe, with the decoded size passed in), but compression writes a different, non-LZ4 format and the API differs

gotchas: Compression refuses (returns 0) any input it cannot shrink by at least an eighth; callers must store the raw bytes and track which values are packed. This refusal is also why the packing benchmark shows +820% to +859% over liblz4 on 64 KiB noise: lzvolt declines while liblz4 actually encodes.

Size the output buffer with lzvolt_decompress_bound(declared), not the exact length, to get the measured speed; the exact length is safe but takes the slower trimmed final copy (34% on incompressible 4 KiB).

Decoders do unchecked copies; safety rests on the validation pass, which the author fuzzes, runs under Miri and tests the assembly under AddressSanitizer. In the log, a 2026-09-20 x86 kernel port mis-decoded 9 of 5760 liblz4 blocks (caught by the refuse-and-fallback path), and an interop test sat red for a day because the routine check ran without --features liblz4.
Throughput figures are counted against unpacked bytes, so a better ratio raises the reported GiB/s; lzvolt_backend() names the code path in use and should be logged next to any measurement.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick lzvolt over LZ4 when you compress small values one at a time and control both the writer and the reader, or when you already store raw LZ4 blocks and want a faster decoder for them. ZXC, misa77 and LZAV publish larger decode margins over LZ4 on file-sized corpora; lzvolt is the one built and measured specifically for 512 B to 64 KiB values.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's Criterion run (docs/MEASUREMENTS.md, 'The standardised run on ad7d338'), on 4-vCPU GCE VMs with Xeon 8481C, EPYC 9B14 and Neoverse V2, rustc 1.85 with fat LTO, lzvolt decoded its own format 14% to 83% faster than Debian 12's apt liblz4 (LZ4_decompress_safe) on all 18 cells of generated JSON-record data (512 B, 4 KiB, 64 KiB); medians of three. On the same LZ4 blocks it was ahead on 20 of 27 cells (worst noise_512, -15% on Xeon), and its packing was faster on 25 of 27 cells against LZ4_compress_default.
status_note: Active single-author project, first released as 1.0.0 on 2026-09-27 (263 commits, 0 stars, 11 crates.io downloads, no issues filed); Apache-2.0 and copyable, but the measured revision ad7d338 is not in the public history and the GCE script references monorepo pieces this repo does not ship.
